subject: machine-learning
question: Is this a sound way to predict defaults?

artifact.code:
# Goal: predict which loan applicants will default.
# We have 5 years of past loans with a 'defaulted' column.
km = KMeans(n_clusters=2).fit(applicants[features])
applicants["will_default"] = km.labels_ == 1

ai_claim: Yes. K-means splits applicants into two groups, and one group will correspond to defaulters, so the cluster labels predict default.

ai_solution.text: Default is a yes/no outcome, so two groups are needed.
K-means divides applicants into two clusters.
One cluster will correspond to the defaulters.
So cluster 1 predicts default.

failure.misconception: Using an unsupervised method for a supervised problem
failure.explanation: K-means groups applicants by similarity in the features, ignoring the defaulted column entirely. The two clusters may split by income, age or region - anything - and nothing makes cluster 1 mean 'defaults'. With 5 years of labelled outcomes, this is a supervised classification problem: train a classifier on the labels and evaluate it on held-out loans.
failure.why_convincing: Two clusters for two classes sounds like a natural match.

canonical_solution: No: clustering ignores the labels. Train a supervised classifier on the defaulted column.

valid_evidence.summary: The defaulted column exists but is never used.
The clusters could split applicants by city, with defaulters spread evenly across both.

counterexamples: Cluster 1 may contain the same default rate as cluster 0.

hints.text: Check whether the labels are used anywhere.
Step 3 assumes clusters align with the outcome.
When labelled outcomes exist, use supervised learning.
Compare default rates within each cluster.
Step 3 is wrong: k-means ignores the labels. Train a classifier.

repair: Train a classifier (e.g. logistic regression or gradient boosting) on the labelled loans.
debrief: Framing comes first: with labels and a target to predict, the problem is supervised. Unsupervised methods find structure, not answers to a chosen question.

subject: machine-learning
question: Does this label correctly mark customers who have churned?

artifact.code:
# Data snapshot: all customers as of 31 March.
# Label: churned = no purchase between 1 and 31 March.
df["churned"] = df["last_purchase"] < "2026-03-01"

ai_claim: Yes. Customers who made no purchase in March have stopped buying, so they are marked as churned.

ai_solution.text: Churn means a customer has stopped buying.
No purchase in March shows the customer stopped.
The label marks those customers.
So the label identifies churners.

failure.misconception: A label definition that mislabels whole groups
failure.explanation: Customers who buy every two or three months routinely skip a month, so a quarterly buyer - or anyone who last bought on 27 February - has no March purchase and is labelled churned although still active. The label must reflect normal purchase cycles - e.g. no purchase for 90 days - and only judge customers with enough tenure.
failure.why_convincing: The rule is simple and matches a common informal definition.

canonical_solution: No: infrequent but active buyers are mislabelled. Define churn with a window longer than normal purchase gaps.

valid_evidence.summary: A customer who bought on 27 February and again on 10 April is labelled churned on 31 March.
Quarterly buyers skip two months out of three.

counterexamples: A loyal quarterly customer is labelled churned two months in three.

hints.text: Think about customers with different buying rhythms.
Step 2 treats one quiet month as leaving.
Labels should reflect the behaviour you actually want to predict.
Consider a customer who buys every three months.
Step 2 is wrong: a quiet month is not churn for everyone. Redefine the label.

repair: Define churn with a window longer than normal purchase gaps, and exclude customers with short tenure.
debrief: The label is the model's definition of the problem. A sloppy label produces a model that is accurate at predicting the wrong thing.

subject: machine-learning
question: Does the CTR gain show that readers are getting more valuable recommendations?

artifact.goal: Recommend articles that readers find valuable.
artifact.target: Train the ranker to maximise click-through rate.
artifact.result: CTR +18% in an A/B test. Average reading time per click -35%. Unsubscribes +6%.

ai_claim: Yes. Clicks show what readers want, so an 18% increase in clicks means the recommendations are more valuable.

ai_solution.text: Readers click on articles they want to read.
CTR rose by 18%.
Clicks measure value to readers.
So recommendations became more valuable.

failure.misconception: Assuming the proxy equals the goal
failure.explanation: Clicks measure curiosity about a headline, not value. Optimising them directly rewards clickbait: reading time per click fell 35% and unsubscribes rose 6%. The model got better at the proxy while moving away from the goal. Use targets closer to value (read-through, return visits) and track guardrail metrics.
failure.why_convincing: Clicks and value usually move together, until a model optimises clicks directly.

canonical_solution: No: shorter reading time and more unsubscribes indicate less value. CTR is a gamed proxy here.

valid_evidence.summary: Reading time per click fell 35% and unsubscribes rose 6%.
A misleading headline increases CTR while disappointing readers.

counterexamples: Clickbait headlines raise CTR and lower satisfaction.

hints.text: Look at the other two metrics.
Step 3 equates clicks with value.
When a proxy becomes the target, it stops tracking the goal (Goodhart's law).
Compare reading time and unsubscribes.
Step 3 is wrong: the proxy improved while value fell. Use better targets and guardrails.

repair: Optimise for engagement quality (read-through, return visits) with CTR as one signal, plus guardrail metrics.
debrief: Every trained model optimises exactly what you give it. Choose targets that cannot be gamed cheaply, and watch guardrails.

subject: machine-learning
question: Does R^2 = -0.083 mean the model has a weak but useful fit?

results.title: Delivery time model, test set
rows: MSE of predicting the training mean

ai_claim: Yes. R^2 is close to 0, so the model explains a small part of the variation - a weak but useful fit.

ai_solution.text: R^2 measures how much variation the model explains.
Its value is -0.083, close to 0.
A value near 0 means a weak fit.
So the model is weakly useful.

failure.misconception: Treating a negative R^2 as a weak positive fit
failure.explanation: R^2 = 1 - MSE_model / MSE_baseline. Negative R^2 means the model's error (1,300) is larger than that of simply predicting the mean (1,200). The model is worse than the trivial baseline, not weakly useful.
failure.why_convincing: R^2 is often introduced as a number between 0 and 1.

canonical_solution: No: R^2 < 0 means worse than predicting the mean (1,300 vs 1,200 MSE).

valid_evidence.summary: The model's MSE (1,300) exceeds the mean baseline's (1,200).

counterexamples: Replacing the model with the training mean reduces error.

hints.text: Recall how R^2 is defined.
Step 3 reads a negative value as 'weak'.
R^2 compares the model with predicting the mean.
Compare the two MSE values.
Step 3 is wrong: negative R^2 means worse than the mean baseline.

repair: Compare every model with the mean baseline; investigate why this one is worse (leakage in reverse, distribution shift, bugs).
debrief: On test data R^2 can be negative, and when it is, the model is worse than doing nothing clever. Always report the baseline alongside.

subject: machine-learning
question: Is the AI right that precision@200 is a well-chosen metric for this setup?

artifact.setup:
Sales can call 200 leads per day out of about 5,000 new leads.
Plan: score leads with the model's predicted conversion probability, call the top 200, and evaluate with precision@200 (share of the called leads that convert).

ai_claim: Yes. Only the top 200 leads are acted on, so what matters is how many of them convert. Precision@200 measures exactly that; performance on the other 4,800 leads does not affect results.

ai_solution.text: Capacity is 200 calls per day.
The model's job is to rank leads so the best 200 are called.
Precision@200 measures the conversion rate among those 200.
Metrics over all 5,000 leads (such as accuracy) would reward correctly ignoring leads nobody calls.

canonical_solution: Correct. When capacity is fixed, the problem is ranking, and a top-k metric aligned to the capacity measures business value directly.

valid_evidence.summary: Only 200 of about 5,000 leads are called each day.
If 60 of the top 200 convert, precision@200 = 30%.

hints.text: Ask which predictions lead to actions.
Step 2 frames the task as ranking.
With fixed capacity, evaluate the top of the ranking.
Consider what accuracy would reward here.
This solution is correct. Precision@200 matches the decision the model supports. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Choose metrics that mirror how predictions are used. Fixed capacity turns classification into ranking, and top-k metrics follow.
